case20v1-ethics.lenses:
Jhatpat and the Pre-Ticked Offer

A decision case on ethical lenses

Opening

At 8.00 pm on Tuesday 20 October 2026, Sunetra Chiplunkar shut the door of a glass meeting room in Jhatpat's Pune office and opened a call with four faces on it. As chief product officer she owned one decision, and she had until Friday 23 October to take it. On Monday 26 October marketing would lock the Diwali campaign, which was built around a feature called Auto-Top-Up. Diwali fell on Sunday 8 November. Her chief executive wanted the feature shipped as designed. Her data scientist held a pilot result the board had not yet seen. Marketing had already briefed the agency, and Saket Chitgopekar had told investors that Diwali would be the quarter's strongest fortnight. Sunetra had spent six years building products that people were glad to open, and she was not sure this one still qualified.

Company background

Jhatpat Technologies, founded in Pune in 2021 by Saket Chitgopekar and two classmates, sells small salary advances of ₹2,000 to ₹15,000 to gig and shift workers: delivery partners working for Swiggy, Zomato and Zepto, and warehouse and factory staff in Pune, Bengaluru and Hyderabad. The money comes from two RBI-regulated NBFC partners; Jhatpat is the lending service provider. Disbursal runs over UPI, repayment through UPI AutoPay, and the fee is a flat 3 per cent of each advance, due within 30 days. Jhatpat began with 9,000 delivery partners in Pune, added Bengaluru and Hyderabad in 2023, and spent its second and third years persuading workers who distrusted app lenders that an advance could be small, quick and honest about its price.

In the quarter ended 30 September 2026 Jhatpat had 4.8 lakh active users, 118 employees and gross fee revenue of ₹26.01 crore. It competes with credit lines offered through Paytm and PhonePe and with employer-linked advance products. RBI's digital lending directions require a key fact statement before each loan, and the DPDP Act governs how consent is taken.

The situation

Auto-Top-Up changes what happens after a repayment. The app immediately shows a new advance for the same amount, with the box already ticked, so that one tap accepts it. Sheetal Cherekar, the designer in Berlin, built the flow; that afternoon, as the call began, she wrote that it was the best-converting screen she had shipped. Her brief had been to remove every step between repayment and the next advance, and she had.

From 1 August to 26 September, Sudhanshu Chavarkar in Toronto ran a pilot on 4,200 randomly chosen heavy users (six or more advances in the preceding 90 days), half with the feature and half without. Treated users took 5.6 advances each against 5.0 for the others, a gain of 12.0 per cent. Of the 2,100 treated users, 525 paid at least once seven or more days late; among the 2,100 others, 441 did. Exhibit 1 shows the base these users come from, and Exhibit 2 prices the options in front of Sunetra.

Festival weeks raise demand for cash: gifts, train tickets home and advance rent all fall in the fortnight before Diwali, and workers who would not normally borrow often do. Shalaka Chandgadkar's team in Singapore telephoned 40 heavy users. Twenty-six said they had taken their latest advance to repay or cover the previous one; 14 did not. Marketing needs Sunetra's answer by Friday. The engineering lead in Bengaluru needs from Monday to build anything other than Option A: a week for B, four days for C. The timeline is in Exhibit 3.

The people

Sudhanshu Chavarkar, data scientist, Toronto (10.30 am on the call). He will not put his name to a deck that quotes the revenue and omits the lateness column, and he says eight weeks cannot show what happens over a year.

Shalaka Chandgadkar, customer-success lead, Singapore (10.30 pm). Most of the workers she calls thank Jhatpat for being there when a salary is late. She is uneasy that the app, not the user, now decides when the next loan starts.

Saket Chitgopekar, co-founder and chief executive, in Jersey City (10.30 am). Borrowers are adults, he argues, rivals will copy the feature, and the board plan assumes a Diwali lift, and he has already told investors so.

Suyash Chunekar, who runs the Dubai family office holding 22 per cent of Jhatpat (6.30 pm). He wants growth, has watched lenders in the Gulf lose their standing with regulators, and asks what Sunetra would be content to see described in a Mumbai newspaper.

Fee is 3 per cent of an average advance of ₹4,000, ₹5,000 and ₹6,000 in the three segments. The total fee is a pooled average (₹2,601.0 lakh over 16,58,400 advances); the total late rate is pooled over all users. Late means any advance repaid seven or more days after its due date.

Option A applies the pilot's 12.0 per cent gain in advances to the 3 to 5 and heavy segments (₹912.6 + ₹1,285.2 = ₹2,197.8 lakh; 12.0 per cent of it is ₹263.7 lakh) and adds the pilot's 4-point lateness gap to the heavy segment's 23.0 per cent. The pilot covered heavy users only. Its users were selected on advances in the 90 days to 31 July and observed over eight weeks, whereas Exhibit 1's segments are quarter-based; that is why the control arm's 21.0 per cent eight-week late rate differs from the quarter's 23.0 per cent. Option B's 4.0 per cent revenue gain (of the same ₹2,197.8 lakh base) and 2-point fall in lateness are Sudhanshu's modelled estimates, not pilot results. Lateness is modelled for the 84,000 heavy users only.

Exhibit 3. The three working days before the campaign locks, and the Diwali date they serve.

The options

Option A: ship Auto-Top-Up as designed on 26 October. The pre-ticked offer appears after every repayment for users with three or more advances in the quarter. It adds ₹263.7 lakh a quarter on the team's estimate, needs no further build, and is modelled to put 3,360 more heavy users into late repayment. It leaves the interface exactly as Sheetal drew it, and the fee and lender terms as they are.

Option B: ship with guardrails on 2 November. The offer appears unticked, shows the fee in rupees on the button, and stops after four advances in any 30 days. It costs ₹18.0 lakh to rebuild, adds ₹87.9 lakh a quarter on Sudhanshu's estimate, and models 1,680 fewer heavy users paying late. The fee stays at 3 per cent.

Option C: do not ship. Jhatpat instead adds a read-only repayment plan to the app and rewrites the Diwali campaign around it, at a cost of ₹12.0 lakh. Revenue and lateness stay where Exhibit 1 puts them, no user sees a new offer, and the plan's Diwali lift is left unmet.

Questions for discussion

  1. What do Exhibit 1 and the pilot show about who generates Jhatpat's revenue, and what the feature does to them?
  2. Apply each of the five Markkula lenses (rights, justice, utilitarian, common good, virtue) to Option A. What does each notice that the others miss?
  3. For each option, whose interest does it serve most directly, and whose does it leave unprotected?
  4. Which option would you take by Friday, which lens carries most weight in your choice, and what evidence would make you change it?

A note for the learner

The Markkula Center's five lenses are questions, not verdicts. Rights asks whom the decision treats as a means; justice asks who carries the burden and who collects the benefit; the utilitarian lens counts total good and harm; the common good asks what the decision does to a shared system; virtue asks what kind of company repeats the act. Their value is that they often disagree, and a decision examined through one alone has not yet been tested. Used well, the lenses are applied to the same facts in turn, with each stakeholder's claim given its due, before any option is chosen.

One defensible path is Option B. On rights, a pre-ticked box turns silence into consent, which sits badly with a consent regime that expects a clear affirmative act; the unticked offer and rupee fee restore that act. On justice, the 84,000 heavy users are 17.5 per cent of users but supply 49.4 per cent of fee revenue and carry the highest late rate, 23.0 per cent. On the utilitarian count, Option B gives up ₹175.8 lakh a quarter against A (263.7 less 87.9) but leaves 5,040 fewer heavy users late (22,680 less 17,640). The common good points the same way: a lender that is seen to engineer repeat borrowing invites the regulator's attention to the whole category. Virtue asks Suyash's newspaper question, and B can answer it.

Sunetra would take B to the board with Exhibits 1 and 2 intact, and commit to a review at eight weeks: if the heavy segment's late rate, measured over a full quarter, is above 23.0 per cent, she halts the feature. A reader who weights revenue more heavily may still defend a different path, but must say which lens has been set aside, and why. Because Exhibit 2 holds estimates, any chosen path should arrive with a stated condition for reversing it.
case40v1-ethics.lenses:
Kalrav Technologies: The Third Tier

A Pune company's voice agent recovers loans better than people do. On Sunday night its product head has five options, two exhibits that disagree, and a blank slide.

1. Sunday night, Aundh

The pandal two lanes from Titiksha Deulkar's flat in Aundh had run its Navratri loudspeakers since seven. Dussehra fell on Tuesday, her board met on Thursday the 22nd, and slide seven of the eleven she had promised them was blank under a heading typed on Friday: Tier 3 — recommendation.

Deulkar was vice-president of product at Kalrav Technologies Private Limited, a 214-person company whose voice agent spoke to borrowers in nine Indian languages for twelve lenders and three insurers; Figure A shows where its people and Monday's two customers sit. The agent told borrowers an instalment was due, offered a date, took a UPI Autopay mandate, and escalated through three tiers of wording as the days past due mounted. Exhibit 1 gives the tiers.

On her screen was a forty-one-second clip in Marathi, one of twenty that Tungnath Dhekane, chief risk officer at Kanchanmala Finance Limited in Nagpur, had sent her on Tuesday the 13th under an undertaking to delete them by the 20th. In it a schoolteacher in Solapur, nineteen days past due on a personal loan of ₹64,000, was told by a voice indistinguishable from a polite young man that her outstanding was visible to her two guarantors, and her record readable by anyone in her block who pulled a bureau report. She cleared the dues on the twenty-fourth day — with money borrowed at five rupees per hundred a month from a lender in her own street, says the consumer commission notice of 29 September.

Deulkar had written the specification for that tier in January 2024. She had also written the line item descoped from it.

2. Kalrav, 2019 to 2026

Tirthraj Dighe and two classmates founded Kalrav in February 2019 around a Marathi and Hindi speech model built for a Nashik co-operative bank that could not staff an evening call desk. FY26 revenue was ₹28.90 crore. It sold on a claim: tele-callers reach a borrower two or three times in a month at best, and the agent reaches them whenever they will answer, inside a 9 a.m. to 6 p.m. window.

Two decisions govern tonight. In November 2023, to win Kanchanmala against a bid on Gupshup's stack, Dighe accepted two terms: one tying part of the fee to measured recovery uplift rather than seats or minutes, which Exhibit 5 prices; the other putting the agent on the lender's premises, every recording staying in Nagpur and Kalrav seeing only metadata. In December 2023 Kanchanmala asked for a harder third tier. Deulkar specified it with a per-tier switch, so a lender could retire one rung without the ladder. The switch was descoped in the same sprint to hold the 9 February go-live, and never re-planned.

So tonight Kalrav cannot turn off one tier. It can turn off a language.

3. The industry

Small-ticket unsecured lending in India had spent three years industrialising its plumbing. Disbursal ran through co-lending and the account aggregator framework; collection through NACH e-mandates and UPI Autopay on NPCI rails; reporting to TransUnion CIBIL within days. The Reserve Bank's digital lending directions put conduct on the regulated entity, not its technology vendor, so Kalrav's exposure was contractual rather than regulatory — and every clause of the Kanchanmala agreement had been drafted by people who knew that. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act added notice, purpose limitation and a consent the borrower could withdraw.

Kalrav competed with Gupshup, Jio Haptik, Exotel and Ozonetel, and with Infosys and TCS whenever a bank decided contact-centre modernisation was a programme rather than a product; its pitch was vernacular quality and recovery outcomes. Kanchanmala was its largest customer, with ₹7,840 crore of assets under management across a two-wheeler book of ₹3,120 crore, a personal-loan book of ₹2,960 crore and a gold-loan book of ₹1,760 crore. Dussehra on 20 October and Diwali on 8 November 2026 would drive disbursal, then delinquency into December. Abroad there were five people in New Jersey, a lead in Singapore, and the Dubai term sheet Exhibit 5 shows unsigned.

Figure A — where the decision sits

Figure A. Headcount at 30 September 2026; the nine figures sum to 214. Dashed boxes are customers, not offices. Offsets are those in force on 18 October 2026, before the European and North American clock changes.

4. What happened, and what was believed

In January 2026 Daundkar's team in Toronto proposed a pacing model: instead of a fixed reminder calendar, let a model choose the next contact interval and the wording variant, trained on one objective, the day-30 cure rate. Version three shipped on 2 March in four languages. Exhibit 6 gives the sequence.

On 1 July, Kanchanmala opened the agent on its personal-loan book, until then worked by tele-callers alone. Accounts entering day-one delinquency between 1 July and 31 August were randomised 90 per cent to the agent and 10 per cent to the manual process: 46,800 and 5,200 accounts, with outcomes measured to day 30 and closed on 30 September. Exhibit 1 breaks the treatment group down by tier; Exhibit 3 puts both cohorts beside the six months before the pilot.

In September Kalrav's board believed four things: that the pacing model's distress flag slowed the ladder down, that the flag's precision was the 0.81 on its model card, that the agent drew 0.40 complaints per 1,000 calls, and that the holdout was business as usual. Four pieces of evidence have since arrived. Of the 4,118 pilot calls the flag fired on, 3,092, or 75.1 per cent, drew another contact within 24 hours, against 41,207 of the 138,782 it did not fire on, or 29.7 per cent; the dialler log does not record whether a contact was outbound, inbound or manual, nor at which tier. Exhibit 4 re-listens to 120 flagged calls. Exhibit 2 counts the complaints. And Daundkar's memo of Friday the 16th is about the holdout.

Kanchanmala had cut its tele-caller bench by 38 per cent in June and moved what was left onto the agent's exception queue, and the holdout got 1.30 manual calls an account against 2.90 across the January-to-June book. One further experiment nobody designed: between 3 and 30 August a build error stopped Tier 3 firing in Marathi. Of the 1,900 Marathi accounts reaching Tier 3 in those 28 days, 785, or 41.32 per cent, cured by day 30; of the 2,320 reaching it on the pilot's other days, 1,136, or 48.97 per cent, did. Kanchanmala also ran a late-fee waiver across its Maharashtra branches from 7 to 28 August.

5. The people

Titiksha Deulkar, VP product, Pune. Wrote the Tier 3 specification and the switch cut from it. Her third ESOP tranche vests on the Series B. Has not told the board she, not engineering, descoped the switch.

Tirthraj Dighe, co-founder and CEO, Pune. Protect the covenant now, fix the tier in January. His holding dilutes in the round. Has given Karamah verbal comfort on the employer-notification tier.

Tamoghna Dharne, head of engineering, Bengaluru. Three weeks for the switch, six for the distress stop, not both in the same pod cycle. Four open requisitions, 23 per cent attrition. Has not said the Marathi build error was his own pod's, nor that it sat on it eleven days.

Tapendu Daundkar, lead data scientist, Toronto. Exhibit 3's uplift is measured against a holdout that was not business as usual, so the invoice is not the world. First author on a paper about the model. Chose the 90/10 split when Dhekane wanted 50/50; Exhibit 4's sample came only from calls the flag had fired on.

Trishita Dhavalikar, principal designer, Berlin. The question is not what the tier costs but what the product is. Her contract renews in January; her pod costs ₹64.00 lakh a head against Pune's ₹11.50 lakh. Wrote the Tier 3 copy in 2024; has drafted a letter to the board, unsent.

Tarachand Dhempe, customer-success lead, Singapore. Withdraw the tier and lenders route those accounts to field agents on a per-recovery fee. Half his variable pay is renewals. Two of his three small-finance-bank renewals are already signed without the tier.

Trilokesh Dandge, head of enterprise sales, New Jersey. A lender that recovers more lends to more people at a lower rate. ₹74 lakh of his variable pay rides on Karamah, whose term sheet makes the employer-notification tier a condition precedent — a formality, he says.

Tanvangi Dhanwate, compliance officer and data protection officer, Mumbai. The 2024 guarantor-contact clause will not survive a notice test under the DPDP Act; restrict the tier to accounts originated on or after 1 April 2026, when Kanchanmala refreshed its notice. She signs the filings in her own name — and signed off the 2024 clause. Her counsel says "arguable", not "compliant".

App complaints are those whose text or category refers to an automated or recorded call. Kanchanmala's picklist added "automated call conduct" on 1 July 2026; April to June were reconstructed that month by keyword search over free-text tickets. 7. Voices

"The clause pays us for cures above a holdout that got 1.30 manual calls an account where the same book had been getting 2.90. Nobody here knows what the agent does."

Tapendu Daundkar, product review, Thursday 15 October, 21:00 IST / 11:30 in Toronto

"Whose consent is the guarantor line standing on, when was it taken, and who here decided a 2024 loan clause was enough?"

Tanvangi Dhanwate to Titiksha Deulkar, email, Friday 16 October, 07:40 IST

"I am not designing the HR notification. Not because of the law, which I am told is fine in the UAE, but because I would have to make that screen look calm."

Trishita Dhavalikar, #ladder-review, Saturday 17 October, 14:12 IST / 10:42 in Berlin

"Take the tier out and Dhekane does not stop collecting. He puts those accounts in front of field agents on a per-recovery fee."

Tarachand Dhempe, renewals call, Friday 16 October, 18:30 IST / 21:00 in Singapore

"Every point of recovery is a point off the rate the next borrower pays. We are in the business of making a 24 per cent loan a 19 per cent loan."

Trilokesh Dandge, pipeline call, Friday 16 October, 19:00 IST / 09:30 in New Jersey

"114 of my 300 tele-callers went in June and your agent stands where they stood. Shorten the ladder in November and I will read you the service level."

Tungnath Dhekane, minute of a review at Kanchanmala Finance, Nagpur, Tuesday 13 October

8. The options, as Deulkar has them written down

At the top of her notebook page, circled twice: is it the tier?

A. Switch the agent off, language by language, on Kanchanmala's personal-loan book. A configuration change: it can be made on Monday. It takes Tiers 1 and 2 with Tier 3, forfeits the Kanchanmala success fee, and puts the service level in play. Untouched: the two-wheeler book, the other eleven lenders, the ladder's wording, the term sheet.

B. Keep the ladder and build a distress stop that de-escalates when the flag fires. Six weeks of two pods, shipping 30 November; it acts on the distress flag. Untouched: Tier 3's wording, the consent basis, the success-fee clause.

C. Build the per-tier switch cut in 2024 and hand it to every lender, each choosing per language. Three weeks, shipping 9 November, inside the freeze and so needing a waiver. It moves the decision to twelve risk officers. Untouched: what the tier says where a lender keeps it, Kalrav's view, the UAE build.

D. Restrict Tier 3 to accounts originated on or after 1 April 2026. Four days of work. It removes the tier from 6,457 of the pilot's 10,586 Tier 3 accounts and needs a re-consent flow Kanchanmala has not budgeted and Dhanwate puts at eleven weeks. Untouched: the wording for newer accounts, the pacing model, the UAE tier.

E. Sign Karamah on 30 October with the employer-notification tier in scope and put India to the January board. It brings ₹14.00 crore into the FY27 run-rate against the ₹50 crore the Series B requires at 31 March 2027, and ships the tier into a market where Kalrav has placed no calls. Untouched: Tier 3 in India, the ladder, the clause.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

Dates. The board meets in Pune on Thursday 22 October. Kanchanmala's code freeze runs 1 to 15 November, so any build meant to be in place for the festival peak must ship by 31 October. Dhanteras falls on 6 November, Diwali on the 8th; the Karamah term sheet lapses on the 30th.

Engineering. One build at a time: three weeks for the switch, six for the distress stop. Neither lands before the 1 November freeze. A language switches off the same day; there is no per-tier switch to throw.

Contract. Ninety days' notice on any reduction in scope; a service level of 85.00 per cent day-30 cure on the treated population. The recordings are Kanchanmala's; Kalrav holds metadata, and until Tuesday twenty clips.

Money and regulation. ₹50 crore of ARR at 31 March 2027 for the Series B, against ₹39.15 crore signed. Conduct liability sits with Kanchanmala; the DPDP Act governs the guarantor line.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. Exhibit 1 reports a day-30 cure rate of 88.24 per cent and Exhibit 3 reports 80.00 per cent for the holdout. State what population each is measured over, and what the 8.24-point difference does and does not establish.
  2. Exhibit 2 supports more than one complaint rate. Work out every rate its three channels and two denominators allow, and say which the schoolteacher would recognise as her own risk.
  3. Exhibit 4 pools to 70.8 per cent against the model card's 0.81, and Daundkar blames language mix. Test that against the exhibit's own figures.
  4. Exhibit 5 prices the success fee against the randomised holdout. Recompute it against Exhibit 3's January-to-June cohort, and decide which party carries the difference, from which date.
  5. The Marathi build error produced a 7.65-point gap in Tier 3 cure rate. What would you need before treating that as a measurement of Tier 3 — and what is the holdout itself, as an object, if the agent works?
  6. Deulkar's list holds five options. Three other things could change instead: the clause that prices the uplift, Kalrav's sight of what follows a cure, and who is randomised into what. Argue which is the real object of Monday's decision; then say what Deulkar should do on Monday morning and what she should tell the board on Thursday about the term sheet lapsing eight days later.

11. Sunday night, continued

At ten the loudspeakers stopped and Deulkar could hear the lane again. She had the clip open, the clause open, Daundkar's memo open, and slide seven still blank. Dighe had asked on the phone what she could honestly ship by the 31st, which was a kinder question than the one she had been asking herself since Tuesday.

She typed a heading into slide seven, read it, deleted it. Below the five options she had written a sixth line on Friday and struck it out so heavily that she could no longer read it. The clips had to go on the 20th.
exp40v2-ethics.lenses:
Ethical Lenses in Practice: What the Framework Decides, and What It Only Documents

A near-expert treatment of the Markkula five-lens method — its lineage, the welfare arithmetic hiding inside its utilitarian lens, the organisational seams where it quietly dies, and the disagreements that remain genuinely open.

1. Two rooms, ten days apart

On 3 February 2026, Nandita Bhargava, VP of Product at Saindhav Health Intelligence in Hyderabad, received a validation report she had waited four months for. Saindhav's early-warning model flags patients likely to deteriorate within six hours; it ran across 46 hospitals and some 2,10,000 monitored admissions a year, an ARR over ₹17 crore. Version 4 beat version 3 on every headline measure: sensitivity rose from 0.71 to 0.80, meaning about 6,720 of the year's roughly 8,400 true deterioration events caught instead of 5,964 — some 756 more catches. Two hospital chains, eleven facilities and ₹4.2 crore of the book between them, had made the v4 numbers a condition of renewal on 31 March.

The report's fourteenth page carried a subgroup table. Among patients over 70 with chronic kidney disease — about 9% of admissions, some 18,900 a year, at a higher event rate of 7.5% — sensitivity moved the wrong way, 0.74 down to 0.66: 936 of that subgroup's 1,418 events caught where v3 caught 1,049, or roughly 113 additional missed deteriorations a year in the frailest population Saindhav served. Dr. Farhan Siddiqui, the clinical lead in Pune, gave the reason: the new training corpus was weighted toward private multi-speciality partners signed in 2025, whose patients skewed younger and less renally impaired. Nandita's question was not whether v4 was better. It plainly was, in aggregate. Her question was whether "better in aggregate" was the right sentence to evaluate at all.

Ten days later, Rohit Deshmukh, Head of Product at Uppalam Commerce in Ahmedabad, faced a different arithmetic. Uppalam ran a B2B marketplace for construction materials — about 1,40,000 dealers, annualised GMV near ₹6,800 crore — alongside a ₹1,150 crore embedded working-capital book. The proposal, "Bharosa Score," would fold repayment behaviour on that book into search ranking: any dealer more than fifteen days past due would be demoted, losing an estimated 38% of order flow until they cured. Ira Nambiar, the risk lead in Bengaluru, modelled on-time repayment rising from 88.4% to 93.1% and credit losses falling about ₹41 crore a year. Zoya Kazmi, who ran the marketplace side, had two objections that did not fit the model: of the 6,200 dealers past due, roughly 2,700 were late because their own buyers had not paid them; and buyers reading a badge called "Bharosa" would take it to describe delivery reliability, when it would substantially describe whether a dealer had repaid Uppalam.

Neither is a compliance question. Saindhav's v4 breaks no Indian regulation; Uppalam's ranking sits inside the Reserve Bank's digital lending guidelines, which say nothing about search rank. In both, the law is silent, the money is clear and the disagreement in the room is real — the territory the Markkula framework was built for.

2. The idea, its lineage, and who refuses to sign it

The ethical lenses framework is a decision procedure requiring that one proposed action be evaluated in sequence from five distinct normative traditions — utilitarian, rights, justice, common good, virtue — with the results recorded separately rather than collapsed into a verdict. Its canonical statement is "Thinking Ethically: A Framework for Moral Decision Making," written at Santa Clara University's Markkula Center for Applied Ethics by Manuel Velasquez, Claire André, Thomas Shanks and Michael J. Meyer, circulated from 1988; the Center's technology-ethics programme, associated with Shannon Vallor, Irina Raicu and Brian Patrick Green, adapted it for software and then for machine-learning systems.

The problem it solves is not that people do not know ethics. It is that applied ethics had produced a stalemate between well-defended monist theories, while those who had to decide — hospital ethics committees, then engineers — needed something usable within an afternoon. The method is deliberate procedural pluralism: it does not claim the five traditions are compatible or commensurable, only that a decision-maker who has asked all five questions is less likely to be captured by whichever one the institution speaks natively. In a product organisation that native language is aggregate welfare with the losses omitted. It helps to see the five as claims a philosopher would sign — and what each refuses to sign, since the refusals are where product arguments break.

LensLineageIt will signIt will not sign
UtilitarianBentham, Mill; today Singer, and cost-benefit analysis"The option producing most total well-being, counting every party equally, wins.""Some options are off the table however good the totals look."
RightsKant, Locke; in law the UDHR, GDPR, India's DPDP Act 2023"No person may be used merely as a means to others' benefit; consent must be real.""A large enough benefit to many licenses overriding one person's autonomy."

Two facts are usually omitted. The Center has treated the list as unstable — a care-ethics lens from Gilligan and Noddings appears in some versions and not others — so a framework whose own authors add and remove lenses should not be taught as a closed axiom system. And its real competitor in industry is not another philosophy but principle lists: NITI Aayog's Responsible AI for All (2021), IEEE's Ethically Aligned Design, the EU AI Act's risk tiers. The lenses differ in kind — they generate questions, not verdicts, at once their strength in a novel situation and their weakness as governance.

Figure 1. Both proposals are supported by one lens apiece and opposed by at least three — but Saindhav's supporting lens is the utilitarian one and Uppalam's is not, which changes what each team has to argue about.

3. Mechanics, including the arithmetic nobody writes down

Expert practice differs from novice practice in four places, three before any lens is applied. The first is framing the unit of decision: "should we ship v4" is not decidable, "should we ship v4 everywhere with no subgroup routing" is. Novices frame at project level, which lets every lens shrug. The second is enumerating stakeholders past the P&L: Nandita's first list had clinicians, hospitals and Saindhav; Farhan added general-ward and elderly-CKD patients as separate entries, and that disaggregation is what lets the justice lens say anything at all. The third is generating the option set, because a review with one option is a ratification ceremony. Saindhav's was four: ship v4 everywhere; hold v3; route elderly-CKD patients to v3 through a fallback ensemble, costing seven weeks and ₹1.1 crore and missing the renewal date; or shift the subgroup threshold, buying sensitivity with false alerts.

The fourth is the utilitarian lens itself, the only one with real formal apparatus and the one teams run most crudely. Written properly it is a weighted sum: total welfare is the sum over groups of a weight times that group's welfare change. Standard practice sets every weight to 1 and calls the result "expected value." Welfare economics names the parameter being silently set — the inequality-aversion parameter ε, from the Atkinson family of social welfare functions, where a group's weight is its welfare level raised to the power −ε. At ε = 0 every life counts the same however badly off the person already is; as ε rises, gains to the worst-off count for more; as ε approaches infinity you reach Rawlsian maximin.

Saindhav's numbers make this concrete. Take a conservative translation: roughly one in nine missed deteriorations outside the subgroup progresses to a preventable death, and one in five inside it. Version 4's 869 additional catches outside are then about 96 deaths averted; its 113 additional misses inside are about 23 deaths caused. Assign baseline health-state indices of 0.78 for the general population and 0.42 for elderly-CKD, from Saindhav's own outcome registry. The comparison now depends entirely on ε.

Three second-order effects follow. The most valuable output is often not a decision but the discovery of a parameter the organisation has been setting by accident: Nandita's memo could now say "we are implicitly at ε = 0, and no clinician here would defend that in writing." The argument then relocates productively — from "is v4 ethical" to whether elderly-CKD patients warrant a weight above 2.3, which clinicians can address. And making a trade explicit does not make it disappear: the fallback forgoes averted deaths during the delay and permanently maintains two models. The lenses convert a hidden trade into a visible one. That is the whole product.

Uppalam's arithmetic shows the same discipline of counting the omitted term. Ira's ₹41 crore of avoided credit loss assumed dealers stayed. Zoya's exit model put attrition among the 2,700 receivable-squeezed dealers at about 640 over two quarters — roughly ₹18 crore of lost GMV contribution and ₹9 crore written off — so ₹41 crore gross becomes ₹14 crore net. A variant exempting dealers whose delinquency traced to verified unpaid invoices lifted repayment only to 91.2%, saving ₹24 crore, but shed only ₹6 crore in exit costs: about ₹18 crore net. The more just design was the more profitable one — a happy contingency, not a law. A practice that survives only when ethics and revenue agree is not a practice.

4. When it applies, stated as testable claims

The framework earns its keep under four checkable conditions. One: the decision is discrete, with an identifiable set of affected parties. Saindhav passes cleanly — one release, two patient groups, a countable effect; Uppalam passes with strain, since the affected set includes buyers who never see the mechanism. Two: the law is silent or merely permissive. Both pass. Three: at least two lenses disagree. If all five converge immediately the exercise was ceremony. Both pass emphatically. Four: someone in the room can change the decision. Saindhav passes — Nandita controls the release train. Uppalam is doubtful: the credit book reports to the CFO and the ranking to Rohit, and no one owns the joint decision. Claim four fails most often and is checked least.

It is actively misleading in three situations. Where harm is diffuse and cumulative — an engagement loop whose damage accrues over eighteen months — a single sitting gives each increment a clean bill of health and misses the trajectory. Where the decision is a bright-line prohibition, five lenses invite a balancing conversation about something that should never have entered the trade space. And where the organisation cannot act on the conclusion, a thorough review manufactures documented knowledge of a harm it then causes anyway — worse than ignorance, morally and legally.

5. Hard edge cases and the organisational seams

Two-sided markets break the utilitarian lens: "net good" is ill-defined when winners and losers are both your customers. Uppalam's demotion transfers value from dealers to buyers and to its own lending book; the firm-level total can be positive while the marketplace becomes, for one side, a worse deal. Experts run the lens twice, once per side, and refuse to sum — a move with no theoretical justification and much practical value.

Regulated contexts invert the sequence. At Nunbandar Exchange, a Mumbai payments and lending platform, counsel's reading of RBI's digital lending guidelines legitimately comes first, because a prohibition removes options rather than weighing them. The failure is the opposite: treating the legal floor as a ceiling. The diagnostic is whether anyone can name a lawful practice the company declines anyway. If not, the firm has no ethics function, only a compliance function with an ethics budget line.

Hardware-plus-software raises irreversibility as a rights problem. When Kharaghoda Instruments, which makes cold-chain telemetry units fitted to about 11,000 refrigerated vehicles, considered a firmware update rejecting third-party calibration probes, the utilitarian case was ordinary — ₹31 crore of service and consumable revenue against marginally better accuracy. The rights lens raised what the software analogy hides: a customer who bought in 2023 cannot decline the update and keep the product working. Ownership has already transferred, and a remote change is closer to entering someone's property than to shipping a release.

AI-native products break the stakeholder step, because the affected subgroup may not exist as a category until the model is measured. Saindhav is the mild version; Agariya Field Systems, below, the severe one. Enumeration cannot precede evaluation — it must be iterative. A review conducted once, before training, is structurally incapable of catching the thing most likely to go wrong.

Figure 3. What mature companies do differs from what they publish. The published answer is a review board; the working answer is a named individual who can hold a release and is measured on having done so at least once.

What mature companies actually do has three features. Reviews attach to release gates, not quarterly ceremonies, because a review that cannot delay anything is documentation rather than governance. Dissent is recorded with a name against it. And the review is re-run after launch, because cumulative harm is only observable in production. Firms that do none of these and still publish an ethics charter are sincere and ineffective rather than cynical — harder to detect, and so more dangerous.

6. What separates an expert from a competent practitioner

The lenses are not commensurable, and scoring them is the main failure of trained teams

A competent practitioner builds a scorecard: five lenses, red-amber-green, majority verdict. The expert refuses the summary column, because rights and utility do not share units and a three-to-two split is evidence of nothing. The sign you are reading a scorecard is a memo with a verdict row and no dissent paragraph. The expert's memo has the opposite shape: a short recommendation, then the strongest surviving objection in the objector's own words. Unanimity is likewise a warning, not a result — in most real cases it means an affected party was never entered on the stakeholder list.

The utilitarian lens is not neutral ground — it is a theory with a hidden parameter

The obvious reading is that expected value is the objective baseline and the other four lenses are values laid over it. The expert knows that setting every weight to one is itself a contested position with a name, and that health economics and disaster policy routinely use ε between 1 and 2. The tell is a team that says "let's start with the numbers and then discuss the ethics." The numbers already contain the ethics.

Rights failures hide inside satisfied consent flows

The competent practitioner checks that consent was obtained; the expert checks what it was about. Saindhav's patients consented to algorithmic monitoring; nobody consented to sitting in a subgroup where the algorithm got worse so another subgroup's care improved. The tell is a consent artefact pitched so generally — "AI-assisted clinical decision support" — that it covers any future model, doing legal work and no moral work.

Justice is two questions, and teams reliably answer one

Distributive justice asks who bears the burden. Procedural justice asks whether the process imposing it was fair — whether affected parties had voice and an appeal. Uppalam's dealers had neither. The tell is a design document specifying the rule in detail and the exception path in a sentence. The exception path is where the ethics lives: rules are indifferent to cause and appeals are not.

Common good is not "reputation risk" with better vocabulary

Reputation risk is a private cost borne by your firm; the common good is a shared resource your firm depletes and the whole category pays for. If Uppalam's ranking stops carrying information about reliability, every B2B marketplace's ranking becomes less believable and Uppalam bears a fraction of that. The tell is a common-good paragraph mentioning only the company's own brand; the expert's names the shared thing drawn down and who else pays.

Lens-shopping is the failure of sophisticated organisations, not naive ones

Naive teams skip ethics. Sophisticated teams run all five lenses and then select the one endorsing the decision already made, which is harder to detect because the artefact looks complete. The tell is a memo where four lenses get two sentences each and the fifth — the supportive one — gets four paragraphs with numbers. The countermeasure is assigning lenses to named people before the recommendation exists, so whoever argues justice has a role rather than an opinion. This is also why experts keep the working: six months on, when a harm surfaces in a complaint, the dated memo naming the objection and the objector is the only record of what the firm knew.

The option set determines the answer more than the analysis does

A review with one option is a vote of confidence. The expert's first move is generating a third and fourth, because most ethical tension in product work dissolves under a design change rather than a value judgement — Saindhav's fallback, Uppalam's exemption. The tell is a review that opens with a built feature. The framework is cheap at design time and expensive at launch; its apparent cost mostly measures how late it was run.

Virtue is institutional habit, not individual discomfort

The naive version asks whether anyone feels bad. The expert version asks what capability the organisation is acquiring. A team that becomes skilled at extracting margin from a captive subgroup has built a durable competence that will be reapplied, by different people, after everyone currently uneasy has left. The tell is the defence "we're only doing this once, for this quarter." Organisations do not have once.

7. How it differs by product type and stage

In consumer products the person harmed and the person who can leave are the same, so rights and virtue dominate and exit is a partial corrective. In B2B they separate — a facilities platform is chosen by someone who does not experience it — shifting weight to justice, because the affected population cannot exit a tool their employer mandates. In enterprise software the difference is governance, not substance: the customer's procurement and audit functions ask some of these questions for you — helpful, and a trap, since they ask about data protection and never about distributive effects. Platforms and marketplaces make the common-good lens load-bearing, because the product is a shared institution whose informativeness is the asset. Hardware makes rights load-bearing through irreversibility, and AI products make all five harder, because affected subgroups are discovered empirically rather than designed.

Stage changes the failure mode, not the relevance. At seed and Series A there is no memo; a founder's judgement substitutes for all five lenses, and under survival pressure it defaults to the utilitarian one without anyone noticing the substitution. The intervention is a habit, not a process — one named person whose standing question is "who is worse off if this works." At growth stage, where Saindhav and Uppalam sit, the risk flips to reviews that exist and cannot bind. At scale it flips again, to reviews that bind so thoroughly the argument migrates to whichever forum has none, usually pricing.

8. Three worked examples, including one where the framework failed

Firm and decisionWhat the lenses surfacedOutcome
Kharaghoda Instruments — firmware lockout of third-party calibration probes across 11,000 installed cold-chain unitsUtilitarian favourable (₹31 crore); rights objected on irreversibility for units already sold; common good objected that a locked estate makes independent verification of cold-chain integrity impossibleGrandfathered pre-2025 units; lockout on new units with disclosure at purchase. ₹19 crore instead of ₹31 crore
Didwana Learning — a "streak insurance" upsell shown to students whose practice streak was about to lapseReview run nine months after launch, prompted by a complaint; all five lenses opposed it, three decisively₹6.4 crore of refunds, a rewritten renewal flow, 41,000 lapsed students who did not return
Agariya Field Systems — shift-allocation model for 74,000 facility-management workersReview run on time, before launch. All five lenses passed. Harm occurred anyway14 months of remediation, an appeals function costing about ₹9 crore, and a rewritten review standard

Agariya is the instructive one, because capable people applied the framework properly and it still failed. The team ran all five lenses on the allocation model: did it distribute shifts fairly, did workers consent to telemetry-based scoring, did it raise total earnings, did it corrode the labour market, was it what a decent employer does. Each returned a defensible pass, and none was dishonest — the model did distribute shifts more evenly than the supervisors it replaced, and median earnings rose 6%.

The harm arrived through a mechanism nobody had lensed. Workers whose phones lost connectivity in basement plant rooms were recorded as unavailable, dropped in the ranking and lost shifts. The model was fine; the appeal path did not exist, because appeals were a support process rather than a product feature and so sat outside the unit of decision the review had framed. Roughly 2,100 workers were affected over eleven months, at a median earnings loss near ₹4,400 a month. The failure was in step one: the unit was drawn around the model, when the thing touching workers was the model plus its exception path plus the supervisors' incentives. The recovery was not a better model. It was an appeals function with a service-level commitment, a rule that connectivity gaps default to available, and a standing requirement that the unit of decision include the process by which a person contests it. Five lenses correctly applied to the wrong object return five correct and useless answers.

Across all six the early warnings are properties of the artefact rather than the outcome, which is what makes them usable: you need not know whether a decision was right to notice that its memo has a verdict column, a single author, no named dissent, and one lens written in far more detail than the rest.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

The monist objection. At its strongest, associated with Singer and with most working welfare economists: lens-switching is motivated reasoning with extra steps. If the traditions conflict, at most one is correct, and letting the decision-maker choose which governs after seeing the answers is a method for rationalising anything — and teams demonstrably foreground the lens endorsing their prior. The remedy is to pick the best theory, usually a distribution-sensitive consequentialism with an explicit ε, and apply it consistently. It would be wrong if pluralist review changed decisions more often than monist review — a claim nobody has cleanly tested.

The rights-primacy objection. The Kantian position, echoed structurally in the EU AI Act's prohibited-practices tier: certain options should never enter the trade space, and inviting a utilitarian argument about them is itself the error. Its evidence is that regulatory regimes which work are built from bright lines, not balancing, because balancing is where institutional pressure exerts itself. It would be wrong if bright lines produced systematically worse outcomes at the margin — and Saindhav is a live test, since a rule forbidding any subgroup regression holds v3 and forgoes 96 averted deaths to prevent 23.

The proceduralist objection. The Rawlsian and Habermasian position: content matters far less than governance — who is in the room, who can stop a launch, whose interests have a representative with standing. Its evidence is that identical frameworks produce opposite outcomes in different firms, so the variance lives in the procedure. It would be wrong if well-constituted panels with real authority still converged on harmful defaults — which, on the evidence of several trust-and-safety functions, they sometimes do.

The virtue-ethicist's scepticism. MacIntyre's position, and in practice many senior engineers': a checklist corrodes the judgement it is meant to support. Once an ethics review can be passed it becomes a thing to be passed, and practitioners stop cultivating the perception that would have caught the problem before there was a form. Its evidence is the visible ritualisation of review at large firms. It would be wrong if firms with formal reviews showed measurably fewer post-hoc harms — and we do not know, because harms are reported by the firms being measured.

These four do not resolve into a synthesis, and practitioners should stop pretending they do. The monist is right that the framework permits rationalisation; the proceduralist is right that authority does more work than method; and it remains the best tool available to a decision-maker with one afternoon, no philosopher, and a release on Thursday.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied the framework produces a five-section memo after the design is complete. Someone who has internalised it intervenes at option generation rather than at review, having learned that most ethical tension is a design problem in a philosophical costume. They argue about parameters rather than about ethics — "we are implicitly weighting these groups equally, and I want that stated" rather than "this feels wrong" — converting an unwinnable values argument into a tractable one. They treat their own recommendation as the weakest part of the document, recording the strongest objection in the objector's language. And a harder marker: they have at least once accepted a materially worse commercial outcome and can say what it cost, in rupees, without dressing it as strategy.

12. What each of them decided

Nandita neither shipped v4 as written nor held it. She shipped it with elderly-CKD patients routed to v3 through a fallback ensemble, missed 31 March by five weeks, and went to both chains with the subgroup table and the ε computation in hand. Her reasoning: the utilitarian case was strong only at an inequality weight the company could not defend in writing; the rights lens objected to a trade no patient had agreed to; and the justice lens found beneficiaries and payers to be different people, the payers frailer. One chain renewed on original terms, the other at a 12% discount costing ₹51 lakh. Saindhav now maintains two models — what Farhan calls the honest price of the decision.

Rohit shipped a modified Bharosa Score: dealers whose delinquency traced to verified unpaid buyer invoices were exempt, the badge was renamed and its methodology disclosed including repayment as an input, and a seven-day notice-and-appeal window preceded any demotion. The modelled saving fell from ₹41 crore to about ₹24 crore, and the net, after exit effects, came out higher than the aggressive design's. Rohit is clear the convergence was luck, and that the case would be the same had the numbers gone the other way.

  1. Saindhav's board could have asked Nandita to justify holding a model that saves 96 lives to protect 23. What is the strongest version of that challenge, and which lens answers it — if any does?
  2. Uppalam's more just design was also more profitable. What would you have advised Rohit had the exemption cost ₹12 crore instead, and what does your answer reveal about which lens you treat as the tie-breaker?
  3. Agariya's review passed all five lenses and the harm happened anyway. Whose failure was that — the framework's, the reviewers', or the organisation's — and what specific change to the review standard would have caught it?

13. Going deeper

Accountability for what products do to people
The lenses say what to weigh before shipping; accountability says who answers afterwards.
Auditing your own product
Turns a launch gate into a repeatable practice — the only way cumulative harm is caught.
A framework for ethical persuasion
Narrows the method to influence design, where the rights lens does most of the work.
Habit formation and attention
The mechanism behind the harms the lenses evaluate: you cannot weigh a loop you cannot describe.
The Hook model
The canonical account of habit products — the vocabulary the lenses are most often applied against.
External and internal triggers
Marks where persuasion starts recruiting a user's own anxiety, and the rights lens stops being a formality.
Fogg behaviour model (B = MAT)
Separates motivation, ability and prompt, naming which lever a design pulls and so which lens applies.
Variable rewards
The most contested mechanic in the toolkit — a utilitarian engagement gain colliding with a virtue-lens objection.
Investment and stored value
Lock-in as accumulated user effort — the asymmetry the justice lens examines when exit stops being real.

Ethical Lenses: A Working Tool for the Decision You're Making Right Now

Rights, justice, utilitarian, common good, virtue — five questions to ask before you ship, not five theories to memorise.

A Tuesday afternoon at Zafraan Wellness

On 14 August 2025, Kabir Mehra, VP of Product at Zafraan Wellness — a Bengaluru meditation-and-anxiety-support app with 1.4 million paying subscribers — opened a growth deck titled "Project Sukoon: Annualise the Base." Zafraan sold two plans: ₹399 a month, cancel any time, or ₹3,588 a year, billed once, marketed as "25% off." Of the roughly 90,000 people who signed up each month, only 22% chose the annual plan on their own. The growth team's proposal had two parts. First, make the checkout page default to the annual plan with the box already ticked; a user who wanted to pay monthly now had to notice the tick and uncheck it. Second, send a daily push notification — "Your calm streak breaks in 3 hours. Ananya already meditated today." — to the 252,000 users who had, at some point, used Zafraan's in-app anxiety check-in feature, a group the product team internally called "flagged."

The forecast was specific: the pre-ticked default would lift annual take-up from 22% to 52% of new sign-ups, adding an estimated ₹9.2 crore a year in upfront, guaranteed cash. The streak notifications, aimed at the flagged cohort, were projected to raise daily engagement in that group by 34%. Kabir had eleven days before the feature was scheduled to ship in the September release train, and a board meeting on the 26th where the CFO wanted the annualisation number in the deck. He did not have a rule that told him what to do. What he had, from a two-day workshop Zafraan's legal counsel had once attended at Santa Clara University's Markkula Center for Applied Ethics, was a way of asking the question five different ways before answering it once.

The idea: five questions, not one

The ethical lenses framework is a decision tool that asks a practitioner to evaluate one proposed action from five distinct ethical traditions in sequence, rather than from whichever tradition happens to be the room's default. It was developed at Santa Clara University's Markkula Center for Applied Ethics, originally written up as "A Framework for Thinking Ethically" by Manuel Velasquez, Claire André, Thomas Shanks and Michael J. Meyer in the late 1980s and refined repeatedly since, most recently for technology and product decisions by the Center's Internet Ethics Program in the 2010s. It exists because a single ethical vocabulary — usually "does this make the business more money" or "is this legal" — tends to feel complete from inside the room and incomplete from outside it. The five lenses are: rights (does this respect everyone's autonomy, consent and privacy), justice (does this distribute benefit and burden fairly across similarly situated people), utilitarian (does this produce the greatest net good once every stakeholder's gains and losses are honestly counted), common good (does this strengthen or corrode the shared trust that lets a whole category of product function), and virtue (is this the kind of thing a person or company of good character would do, repeatedly, in public). The sentence Kabir could say in the boardroom without sounding glib was this: we haven't finished the ethics of a decision until we've asked all five lenses, not just the one that already agreed with us.

Figure 1. The five lenses surround one decision. Each answers a different question about the same fact pattern; none of them is a vote, and their answers are not meant to be averaged.

How Kabir actually ran it

The mechanics practitioners usually skip sit before and after the five questions themselves. First, name the decision at the right level of specificity — not "should we grow annual subscriptions" but "should checkout default to a pre-ticked annual box, and should guilt-framed notifications go to users who have disclosed anxiety." Vague framing lets every lens give a shrug; precise framing forces a real answer. Second, list every stakeholder affected, not just the ones already in a revenue model — Kabir's first list had only "subscribers" and "shareholders" until his colleague Meera Iyer, Zafraan's clinical advisor, added "the 252,000 flagged users specifically" and "everyone who has ever recommended a wellness app to an anxious friend." Third, after running all five lenses, look for convergence before looking for a tie-breaker, because a framework this open-ended surfaces disagreement far better than it resolves it by force.

Kabir wrote one paragraph per lens, using Zafraan's own numbers rather than abstractions. The rights lens asked whether users understood, at the moment of clicking "Subscribe," that they were committing ₹3,588 for a year; a pre-ticked box that most people don't notice fails that test even if a disclosure exists somewhere in the terms. The justice lens asked who bears the cost of an accidental annual commitment — disproportionately first-time subscribers and, within them, disproportionately the flagged cohort, since anxious users are statistically less likely to contest a charge quickly. The common good lens asked what happens to the wellness-app category's credibility if a company selling calm is discovered manufacturing urgency to sell it — a reputational externality that lands on every competitor, not only Zafraan. The virtue lens asked what habit the growth team was building in itself by treating "streak-shaming a person managing anxiety" as a normal Tuesday tactic. Only the utilitarian lens needed real arithmetic to answer, because only it claims to net everything into one number.

The worked arithmetic: two passes

Pass one used the growth team's own forecast, unmodified. Pre-ticking annual lifts take-up from 22% to 52% of the 90,000 monthly sign-ups — an extra 27,000 people a month choosing annual, mostly by default rather than deliberation — producing the projected ₹9.2 crore a year in upfront cash. Against that, Kabir asked Zafraan's support lead for the refund-dispute rate on forced-continuity designs at comparable apps, a figure the growth team's own risk memo had cited from the Central Consumer Protection Authority's 2023 complaint data: roughly 4% of newly converted annual subscribers request a refund within 60 days once they notice the year-long commitment. Four percent of 27,000 is 1,080 distressed people every month, and because the streak notifications and the checkout default hit the same flagged cohort, that distress concentrates in exactly the 252,000 users least equipped to absorb it. A naive utilitarian tally — ₹9.2 crore of benefit against a support-ticket cost of a few lakh rupees — looks like an easy yes. A fuller tally that monetises 1,080 people a month losing time, trust and, for a meaningful fraction, a genuine anxiety trigger, against the reputational cost if the design became public, turns the same lens from an easy yes into something close to a coin toss.

Pass two removed the pre-tick, replacing it with a clearly marked, equally weighted recommendation, and excluded the flagged cohort from streak notifications entirely. Take-up rose only to 34%, since a recommendation carries a smaller default effect than a silent tick-box — an extra 10,800 people a month, worth about ₹3.9 crore a year, with the refund-dispute rate under 1%. The point of the two passes was not to find the "correct" number; it was to show Kabir that rights, justice, common good and virtue converged cleanly on the modified design in a way the utilitarian lens, alone, never would have forced him to notice.

Eight things a learner has to get past

The lenses are not a vote to be averaged

Getting three lenses green and two red does not mean "proceed, 3–2." The lenses ask structurally different questions; a rights violation isn't cancelled out by a utilitarian surplus any more than a good joke cancels out a bad diagnosis. The output of the exercise is a documented tension, not a score.

The utilitarian lens lives or dies on who counts

Most first attempts at the utilitarian lens only count the stakeholders already inside the spreadsheet — paying users, shareholders. A serious pass adds non-users affected indirectly (a subscriber's family absorbing an unwanted charge), and the category-wide trust cost, which is real but genuinely hard to price and is exactly the number teams are tempted to leave out because it is inconvenient rather than because it is small.

Rights is not the same as legality

Zafraan's terms of service disclosed the annual commitment in clause 14; that satisfied India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act consent requirements and would likely have satisfied a court. It did not satisfy the rights lens, which asks about genuine, noticed consent at the moment of the click — a bar the CCPA's 2023 dark-pattern guidelines explicitly named "forced continuity" for failing to clear, independent of contract law.

Justice splits into two different fairness questions

Distributive justice asks whether the burden of this design falls disproportionately on one group — here, the flagged cohort. Procedural justice asks whether the process that decided this was itself fair — whether Meera, the clinical advisor, had real power to stop the launch or only the right to comment on a deck already scheduled to ship. Teams that answer only the first question miss half the lens.

Common good is not utilitarian aggregation in a category-wide costume

A decision can pass a firm-level utilitarian test — net positive for Zafraan and its subscribers — and still fail the common good lens, because the common good lens asks about the durability of trust in an entire product category, a resource every wellness app draws on and none of them alone owns.

Virtue is not the same as "would I feel bad"

Guilt is an emotion; virtue is a question about character and habit. The relevant question isn't whether the growth lead feels queasy about the streak notification — it's what kind of product organisation repeatedly treating anxious users as a conversion segment turns Zafraan into, whether or not any one person on the team feels anything about it.

The framework clarifies disagreement; it does not resolve it

Nothing in the method ranks the five lenses. When they conflict, a human being still has to decide which tradition should govern this particular decision, and say why — the framework's contribution is making sure that choice is made in the open, on the record, rather than by whichever lens happened to speak first.

It strains against diffuse, cumulative harm

Five lenses applied once work well for a discrete decision with identifiable stakeholders, like a checkout default. They work far less well for harm that accumulates slowly across years of engagement design — a single sitting with five questions can't capture what eighteen months of daily streak notifications do to a population's relationship with an app; that requires the lenses run repeatedly, as an audit habit, not once as a launch gate.

Consumer, B2B, marketplace — and scale

In a consumer product like Zafraan, the person affected by the design and the person who can walk away are the same individual, so the rights and virtue lenses carry unusual weight — there is no intermediary absorbing the ethical cost. In a B2B product like Kesar Works, an HR platform sold to a company's admin team, the person who chooses the persuasive nudge (an HR manager rolling out mandatory "wellness check-in" streaks for 4,000 employees) is not the person who suffers it; the justice lens becomes the load-bearing one, because employees have no realistic exit from a tool their employer has mandated the way a consumer can simply uninstall an app. In a marketplace like Khari Baoli Mandi, a B2B platform matching spice wholesalers with retail buyers, a persuasive design that favours one side — say, defaulting sellers into an exclusivity clause — reallocates value between two paying customer groups rather than extracting it from a captive individual, which makes the justice lens (is this fair between the two sides) and the common good lens (does this erode trust in the marketplace as an institution) do more work than the utilitarian one, since "net good" is ambiguous when the winners and losers are both the platform's own customers.

Scale changes which lens gets exercised, not which lens matters. At an early-stage startup, there is rarely a formal five-lens memo — a founder's intuition stands in for all five lenses at once, and because survival pressure is constant, that intuition defaults to the utilitarian lens by habit, often without noticing the substitution. At a company Zafraan's size, the risk shifts from never asking the questions to asking them ceremonially: an ethics review that exists on the launch checklist but has no power to delay a ship date is procedural justice failing quietly, dressed up as due diligence.

Where the analysis gets faked

The first common mistake is running only the utilitarian lens and calling the result "the ethics review" — the symptom is a slide that says "expected value positive, ship it," and the cheapest diagnostic is to ask, out loud, which of the other four lenses was never written down; if the honest answer is "all of them," nothing was actually reviewed. The second is treating legal sign-off as ethical sign-off — the symptom is "legal says we're DPDP-compliant" ending the conversation, and the diagnostic is the front-page test: would this decision read as fine if a journalist described it accurately and neutrally, compliance certificate included. The third is running the framework only after a controversy breaks, which turns a decision tool into a PR defense; the diagnostic is simply checking whether a dated five-lens memo exists in the launch documentation from before ship day, not after. The fourth is letting whichever lens the most senior person in the room already favours function as the tie-breaker by default — the symptom is a decision memo where four lenses all reach one conclusion and the fifth, conveniently the CEO's favourite, overrules them without anyone naming that as what happened.

What good looks like

Kabir's memo to the board, dated 20 August, ran all five lenses on both passes and recommended the modified design: no pre-tick, a genuine recommendation instead, and the flagged cohort excluded from streak notifications outright. He did not hide the ₹5.3 crore gap between the aggressive and modified forecasts; he named it, alongside Meera's clinical judgment that shaming an anxious person into a habit is a contradiction Zafraan's own brand could not survive being caught in. The board approved the modified design on the 26th, with the CFO noting, on the record, that the smaller number was the honest one.

What Kabir decided, and two questions to sit with

Kabir shipped the recommendation-not-default checkout and the exclusion for flagged users, accepting ₹3.9 crore instead of ₹9.2 crore, because four of the five lenses converged on that design and the fifth — utilitarian — was close enough to a coin toss on the aggressive version that it could not overrule the other four on its own. The natural next step is accountability for what products do to people: the lenses tell you what to weigh before you ship, not who answers for the outcome afterward. Sit with these two questions: which of your last five product decisions used only the lens that happened to agree with the growth target, and if a journalist described your best-performing feature accurately on tomorrow's front page, which lens would you least want them to have asked?
